newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Australia puts weight behind WTO farm statement.
newsitem.headline: Australia puts weight behind WTO farm statement.

text.p: Australian Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer said on Thursday a declaration of goals from this week's World Trade Organisation (WTO) ministerial meeting must include agriculture.
"I would be bitterly disappointed if agriculture did not make it into the conference declaration," Fisher told a news conference, adding he remained overall "quietly optimistic" about the outcome.
Fischer dismissed speculation that agriculture had been overshadowed by other issues such as the Information Technology Agreement (ITA) and labour standards at the WTO conference.
The Cairns Group, a body of free trading agricultural exporting nations, had met on Sunday for a strategy meeting, he said.
"We built on a strategy which we are working through, and which we have not issued a statement on," Fischer said.
Asked whether the Cairns Group intended to issue a statement, he said: "At the end of proceedings, it has been contemplated we will do so."

Canadian Trade Minister Art Eggleton told Reuters there was a good chance of a separate statement by the Cairns Group but that it would not contradict the declaration nor necessarily mean the declaration was unsatisfactory.
"I think there's a good chance to see (a separate statement) but it'll be complementary and supplementary to what's inside of the declaration," he said.
"We haven't finalised it yet but we're talking about it."

The Cairns Group of farm exporting nations, who range from Argentina and Australia to Thailand and Uruguay, wants the WTO delaration to put more emphasis on freer agricultural trade and perhaps a speedier removal of trade barriers.
They are seeking a reference in the declaration to preparations for new WTO farm talks set for the end of the century. But they are opposed by the EU, Japan and South Korea.

As to whether the wording of the declaration itself would be satisfactory on agriculture, Eggleton said: "I think so, but there are so many issues covered in the declaration that for some countries there's not enough mention on the specifics of agriculture. It's not any disagreement with what's in the text."
Australia's Fischer said he was optimistic further progress could be made on liberalising agricultural trade.
"The very best way forward, to boost the standard of living of importing and exporting countries, is by the opening up of agricultural trade liberalisation," Fischer said.
